spoken: Look up on a clear day, and the whole sky glows blue.
But sunlight is white, and the air around you looks perfectly clear.
So where does all that blue come from?
And once you know, a second puzzle appears. Why isn't the sky violet?
The answer takes in a tube of smoke, a fourth power, the sunsets of Mars, and your own eyes.
This is why the sky is blue.
Start with sunlight. It looks white, but it's a mixture of every colour of the rainbow.
Isaac Newton showed this with a prism, which spreads white light out into a spectrum.
Light is a wave, and its colour is set by its wavelength, which is the distance from one crest to the next.
Visible light runs from red, with waves about 720 nanometres long, to violet, at about 380.
A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
In between come orange, yellow, green and blue.
We'll compare blue light at 450 nanometres with red light at 700.
Blue waves are shorter, and the whole story turns on that difference.
People have wondered about the colour of the sky for centuries.
In the early fifteen-hundreds, Leonardo da Vinci guessed that sunlight scattered by tiny particles in the air makes the sky blue.
In 1869, the Irish physicist John Tyndall took the first steps toward a real explanation.
He needed perfectly clean air for his work on heat, and he hunted for dust by shining bright light through it.
When he slowly filled a tube with smoke and shone a beam along it, he saw something striking.
From the side, the beam looked blue. From the far end, it looked red.
The tiny particles were scattering blue light out sideways, and letting redder light carry on.
Tyndall suggested that this is why the sky is blue.
But he couldn't explain why blue light scatters more, and dust alone couldn't explain how blue the sky is.
The explanation began in 1871, with a young British physicist, John William Strutt.
Two years later he became Lord Rayleigh, and the effect now carries his name. It's called Rayleigh scattering.
Light is an electric and magnetic wave. As it passes a tiny particle, its electric field shakes the charges inside.
The shaken particle becomes a tiny antenna, and sends out light of its own in new directions.
This works for particles far smaller than the wavelength, meaning less than about a tenth of it.
And it follows a simple rule, that scattering goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power.
Halve the wavelength, and the scattering gets 16 times stronger.
So compare blue at 450 nanometres with red at 700. The ratio of 700 to 450, raised to the fourth power, is about 5.9.
Air scatters blue light nearly 6 times more strongly than red.
In 1899, Rayleigh showed that the same rule applies to single molecules.
Molecules of nitrogen and oxygen are less than a nanometre across, which is hundreds of times smaller than a wave of light.
So the air itself scatters the light. No dust is needed.
Later, Albert Einstein worked out the scattering by molecules in detail, and his result agreed with experiment.
Now picture sunlight streaming down through the air.
Most of it comes straight through, but some is scattered by molecules on the way.
Because short waves scatter most, it's mostly blue light that gets knocked off in new directions.
That scattered blue reaches your eyes from every part of the sky, so the whole dome glows.
The sunlight that comes straight through has lost a little blue, so the Sun itself looks slightly yellow.
When it's measured, the light of a blue sky holds every colour, with a broad peak between 450 and 485 nanometres.
Our eyes take that mix as blue blended with white, which gives the soft colour we call sky blue.
And no, the sky isn't blue because it reflects the sea. If anything, it's the other way round.
Seen from the beach, the sea looks blue partly because it reflects the sky.
But here's the puzzle. Violet light has even shorter waves than blue.
At 400 nanometres, violet scatters more than 9 times as strongly as red.
So why isn't the sky violet?
Part of the answer is that sunlight holds less violet than blue to begin with.
And some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, before it reaches us.
Still, a rainbow shows that plenty of violet gets through. The rest of the answer is in your eyes.
For one thing, our eyes are less sensitive to violet.
We see colour with three kinds of cone cells, which respond most strongly to red, green and blue light.
Skylight stimulates the red and green cones about equally, and the blue cones more strongly.
Our vision reads that combination as a pale blue.
So the blue of the sky is partly physics, and partly the way we see.
If air turns sunlight blue, why are clouds white?
Clouds are made of water droplets, typically a few micrometres, or thousandths of a millimetre, across.
That's thousands of times bigger than an air molecule, and bigger than a wave of light.
Particles that big don't follow Rayleigh's rule. They scatter all colours about equally.
This is called Mee scattering, after the German physicist Gustav Mee.
Scatter every colour alike, and white light stays white.
A thick cloud reflects 70 to 95 percent of the light that falls on it, across all colours.
Its base can look grey, simply because less light makes it through.
The same kind of scattering makes haze look whitish, and puts a bright white glow around the Sun.
Scattered skylight has another property that our eyes can't see. It's polarised.
Light waves can vibrate in any direction across their path. In polarised light, one direction wins out.
Skylight is most strongly polarised in a band 90 degrees away from the Sun.
There, in a clear sky, the polarisation can reach about 80 percent.
Polarising sunglasses can make that part of the sky look a deeper blue.
Rayleigh's first papers on the sky, in 1871, were titled On the light from the sky, its polarization and colour.
Many insects can sense this pattern and use it as a compass.
The idea goes back to Karl von Frisch's studies of honeybees.
From the pattern alone, an animal can work out where the Sun is, even when it's out of sight.
It has even been suggested that Viking sailors did something similar, with a crystal called a sunstone.
As the day ends, the same rule paints the sky in different colours.
When the Sun is high, its light takes the shortest route through the air.
Squeeze all the air above you to sea-level density, and it would be only about 8 kilometres deep.
Near the horizon, sunlight has to slant through far more air, about 38 times as much.
That's like crossing more than 300 kilometres of air at sea level.
Along that path, the blue and green are scattered out almost completely.
What's left to reach you is orange and red.
That reddened light falls on clouds, and they scatter it back to us, painting red and orange on white.
In very clear air, a setting Sun looks yellow.
Fine particles of smoke or dust make it redder, and sea salt can turn it orange.
And after sunset, ozone high in the atmosphere helps keep the sky overhead blue.
On other worlds, the physics is the same, but the air is different.
At the surface of Mars, the air is only 1 to 2 percent as dense as ours, and full of fine dust.
By day, the Martian sky is a butterscotch colour.
But near the setting Sun, the Martian sky turns blue.
NASA's Curiosity rover photographed a sunset like this in 2015, from Gale Crater.
According to NASA, the fine dust lets blue light through more efficiently than redder colours.
So the blue stays close to the Sun, while yellow and red light spreads across the sky.
It's the opposite of what happens on Earth.
So, why is the sky blue?
Sunlight holds every colour, and the molecules of the air scatter short waves far more than long ones.
Blue scatters nearly 6 times more than red, so scattered blue reaches us from all over the sky.
Violet scatters even more, but sunlight holds less of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
At sunset, the light crosses so much air that the blue is scattered away, leaving orange and red.
And clouds, made of far bigger droplets, scatter every colour alike, so they stay white.
Every patch of blue you see is sunlight that the air itself has turned toward your eyes.
